text: Honestly, the whole reason Cassini had to end up diving into Saturn was to keep it from ending up on one of the moons later. If it had stayed in orbit, a slight drift or collision with Enceladus or Titan could have carried Earth germs with it, and that's exactly the kind of contamination scientists have been worried about. So they used up its fuel and aimed it straight into the planet, where the atmosphere burns it up. It's not a dramatic sacrifice, just basic hygiene for the next spacecraft.

I’d guess the most likely thing is that your stationary leg is doing more work than you realize. When you push, the standing leg isn’t just standing there; it’s absorbing every impact from the road and keeping the board balanced. If you’ve been pushing a lot, the muscles in that leg get tired and can start to ache, especially around the knee or hip. That’s one of the things that always seemed underrated to me: the leg that looks passive is actually doing a lot of stabilizing.

There’s also the question of how you’re pushing. If you’re pushing with a stiff or awkward motion, you can overload one side of the leg. I’ve seen people lean on the standing leg in a way that makes the knee or ankle take a weird angle. That can cause a dull, aching pain rather than a sharp injury. If the pain is in a specific spot, that might point to an existing knee or ankle issue flaring up, but I don’t know your exact spot.

Honestly, the short version is that it usually comes down to overuse or form. Skateboarding is not just about the pushing leg; the other leg has to remain stable and absorb shocks. If you push too hard or too often, you’re basically asking that leg to do double duty. I’d try slowing down, keeping your knees bent, and not forcing your weight onto the standing leg more than necessary. A lot of riders never think about the non-pushing leg until it complains, which is annoyingly common.

If it’s just muscle soreness, it should settle with rest and a bit of stretching. If it’s a sharp or persistent pain, that’s a different story, and you might want to check whether there’s a joint issue underneath. But for a dull ache after a session, I’d bet it’s fatigue and mechanics, not a serious injury.

Honestly, I think the confusion comes from treating "African" like a strict geographic passport. The short version is it's a historical and cultural marker, not a literal birthplace.

Most African Americans have deep roots in West and Central Africa, which is where the transatlantic slave trade pulled the majority of their ancestors from. So when people use the term, it's pointing to that shared continental heritage. It’s a way of acknowledging that deep historical connection to the continent, regardless of where the person actually grew up.

I guess you could call it an umbrella term.

Why does that matter? Because Africa is a massive continent with dozens of distinct ethnic groups and languages. I think using "African" in the name was a way for people in the US to openly claim that heritage, especially after the 1960s and 70s.

It’s a bit of a generalization, and I know it bothers some people because it flattens a lot of specific ethnic identities into one broad label. But as far as I know, that’s the main reason for the naming.

Anyway, it’s mostly about connecting the US population to their broader ancestral roots, even if most of them haven't set foot on the continent themselves.

As far as I know, the main routes have been smuggling across the Turkish and Lebanese borders, plus local workshops that modify what comes in. My understanding is that supply has kept going because the demand never really went away, and once you're in a conflict, the infrastructure is already there. I think that's the annoyingly short version: it depends. I guess that's why the flow persists.

I think the premise is a little too neat. It’s not that every drug is bad, it’s that the effect people want is usually tied to the same brain systems that also drive tolerance and dependence. You can’t just cherry-pick the dopamine hit without the rest of the wiring. That’s the annoying bit: the pleasure signal and the “need more” signal are neighbours, so intensity and risk come bundled together.

Also, “0 adverse effects” is a high bar, especially with the heavy stuff you mentioned. Heroin and coke aren’t just “pleasure machines.” They alter heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, and how you process pain. Even if someone only uses them occasionally, the body still reacts in ways you can’t fully control, and that’s what makes doctors and researchers nervous.

The reason you don’t get a clean, intense euphoria with no downsides is that euphoria is a strong deviation from baseline. Your nervous system is wired to notice deviations and push back, so tolerance builds and the same dose stops delivering the same high. That’s not just a habit forming; it’s a physiological response.

I’d also push back on “why can’t there be a drug with 0 adverse effects” in a different way. There are drugs designed to be safer, but even those still interact with receptors that have other roles. If you target the pleasure pathway hard, you’re almost certainly also hitting adjacent functions. You can lower the risk, but the bundle of effects doesn’t separate cleanly.

So my take is this: the badness isn’t arbitrary. The strong effects people want are connected to systems that also produce adverse outcomes, and the body responds by adapting. You can design safer molecules, but a drug that gives intense pleasure with literally zero adverse effects would have to avoid tolerance and dependence entirely, and that’s the part I think is genuinely hard.

Hi Sam,

I know that tired, aching feeling well, even if it isn't exactly a headache. My guess is it's a mix of walking for hours, not eating properly, and the low-grade stress of keeping up with a shopping spree. Your body starts telling you it's run out of fuel. The pain might also be from muscle tension in your neck and shoulders, or from dehydration, and long days can make that worse. It's not imaginary, and you're not being dramatic. Honestly, the first thing I'd try is eating something and drinking water more deliberately, and stepping away if the pain gets bad.

Cheers,
Alex

Hi Sam,

Good timing on this. My take is that the thing that matters most isn’t the property itself but the paperwork and money trail behind it. That part always seemed like the part people underestimate, and honestly, that’s where a deal can quietly fall over.

For you, I’d make sure you’re checking whether the land has a clean title, because if ownership isn’t clearly in the seller’s name, you can end up buying someone else’s problem. I’d also push for an independent survey before you pay a penny in earnest money. You don’t want to discover later that the plumbing or the structure is a mess.

One more point: budget for the boring costs. Stamps duty, legal fees, and valuation can add up faster than people expect. I’m guessing you already know this, but it’s worth writing it down in a spreadsheet so the total price isn’t a surprise.

Hope that helps.
Best,
Alex

Hi Sam,

Honestly the short answer is: convenience, but you're trading some performance.

A 3-in-1 is basically a single formula that has to clean your body, wash your hair and leave it feeling conditioned. That means the surfactants, conditioning agents and skin cleansers have to work together in one bottle, so each job gets a little watered down. I think that's the big difference from the separate products. You're not getting the dedicated strength of a real shampoo, a real conditioner and a real bodywash; you're getting a compromise that's good enough for most people.

Compared with a 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner, the added piece is the bodywash part. Hair and skin actually want different care: skin needs to be cleansed without being left tight or itchy, while hair needs detangling and softness. Putting both in one product means the formula has to balance those needs, and in practice that often shows up as hair feeling less clean or skin feeling less fresh.

Anyway, I'd use it for travel or quick routines, but I wouldn't expect it to replace everything.

Take care,
Alex

Hi Sam,

Good question, honestly. The short version is that we basically put GPS receivers on bedrock and track their positions over time. That gives millimeter-level movement, but GPS is only at fixed stations, so it doesn’t cover whole plates evenly.

Satellite radar helps fill gaps. InSAR can track deformation over broad areas, which is useful when the ground is shifting in ways you can’t capture with just a few GPS points. As far as I know, the real answer is a combination of both, plus geological and tectonic modeling to turn local measurements into larger plate motion.

My understanding is that this is less about a single “speed” number and more about a mosaic of data. Some places move more obviously than others, and that part always seemed a little dramatic, but it’s also why you can get different “answers” depending on the region and method.

Anyway, I hope that makes sense.

Best,  
Alex

Inbreeding doesn't make every child's IQ drop the same way. The main scientific reason is increased homozygosity. Humans carry small genetic variants that are usually harmless with one copy but harmful with two. When relatives mate, children inherit more identical genetic segments from a shared ancestor, so rare recessive mutations are more likely to appear in two copies. That can show up as lower cognitive performance.

IQ depends on many genes and environment, not one gene. The effect of inbreeding is probabilistic, not deterministic. A child of first cousins has a higher chance of carrying two copies of a harmful variant than a child of unrelated parents, so the average IQ shifts downward.

Inbreeding also increases relatedness, raising the chance that small disadvantages accumulate across many traits, including brain function. It isn't just one 'IQ gene' failing; it is the combined load of hidden mutations becoming visible more often.

Honestly, it mostly depends on what happened and where exactly it hit, but in general the arm just isn't as wired for pain as the torso or head. The upper arm and forearm have a decent layer of muscle, fat and connective tissue that helps cushion impacts, and the nerves there are less densely packed than in the chest, abdomen or neck.

So a cut or graze on the arm often feels more manageable, partly because you can move it away, hold it, and see what's going on. It also matters psychologically: an arm injury feels less threatening to the core of you, so the brain doesn't always treat it the same way. That doesn't mean it doesn't hurt at all, just that it often feels easier to live with than a hit to the body.

The short version is this: carbon monoxide is nasty because it grabs the oxygen carrier in your blood and won’t let go, while carbon dioxide mostly doesn’t. In the blood, haemoglobin is what carries oxygen, and CO sticks to it roughly twenty times more tightly than oxygen does. Once CO is bound there, that molecule can’t carry oxygen properly, so your tissues start starving while you’re still breathing normally. That’s the poison part.

Carbon dioxide behaves differently. It’s something your body makes all the time, and your blood and cells have good ways to handle it. High CO2 can be uncomfortable and affect breathing, but it doesn’t outcompete oxygen for the same binding spot in the way CO does. So in normal indoor air, the amount of CO2 people notice is usually not the dangerous one; CO is the sneaky one.

I guess the practical point for the wiki is that CO is colourless, odourless and hard to detect, which is why a detector is useful. My understanding is that most people equate “gas” with CO2, but the acute poisoning risk from CO is much more severe. CO2 can become dangerous in enclosed spaces at high levels, but that’s a different scenario from breathing CO in a normal room.

Anyway, the key takeaway is that CO blocks oxygen transport, not that it’s just “another gas.” For someone new to the topic, that’s the thing to remember.

I think the scariest part of a crash is the forward momentum. As far as I know, when the plane stops suddenly, your body wants to keep going. The three-point seatbelt stops your chest, but your head keeps moving, which is how you get whiplash or brain injuries. So the brace position is basically about aligning your body to stop that relative movement. I guess it sounds a bit counterintuitive to lean forward when everything is shaking, but that's the whole point.

My understanding is you put your hands on your knees or under your chin, and lean forward. Why does that matter? Because it keeps your head from swinging forward into your chest or the seat in front of you. It also keeps your chest compressed so your heart and lungs aren't taking the brunt of the impact. Honestly, the whole thing always seemed like a lot of fuss to me, but the physics makes sense. You're just stopping your head from doing its own thing.

It’s not a magic shield, but it does cut down on the worst injuries. The flight attendants will tell you exactly which hands-on-knees or chin version to use depending on your seat, so just listen to them. That's about it, really.

Honestly, I think the short answer is that the idea of a recognizable, widespread brand is basically an industrial-era invention. Before that, businesses were mostly local, family-run operations tied to specific people or pieces of land. So when the industrial revolution started shifting everything to mass production and massive capital, those older setups just couldn't keep up. I guess you could say the old guilds and workshops got squeezed out.

They didn't vanish overnight, but the sheer scale of modern retail made the old ways feel obsolete. Anyway, it's why you don't see names like the old Hanseatic League or medieval workshops on today's big corporate lists.

I think the short version is: it depends, annoyingly, on how the numbers are actually calculated. Dealerships can advertise lower interest rates because those rates are often subsidized by the manufacturer, not because the whole deal is cheaper. A low headline rate doesn’t mean you pay less at the end.

What gets lost in the comparison is that the bank’s number isn’t just a rate. If the bank charges origination fees, processing fees, or bundles insurance-like products, those can wipe out a slightly higher rate. My understanding is that the bank often gives you a cleaner, more transparent total: principal, interest, fees, and what you actually pay over the loan term. The dealership’s low rate may come with a package of extras, so the advertised percentage looks better while the actual cost is higher.

Why does that matter? Because the advertised dealer rate can make the deal look attractive, but the buyer has to look past the rate itself. A concrete example: a dealer advertises 2% financing, but the car costs more than the same model bought cash, or the loan includes mandatory add-ons. The bank might offer 4% on the same car at a lower purchase price, and the total paid ends up lower.

The thing is, banks compete on total cost and convenience, while dealerships compete on rate and convenience of buying and financing in one place. That’s why a bank loan can be cheaper even when the dealer’s rate is lower: the bank’s total monthly payment and total cost can come out smaller once you include the car price, fees, and the term length.

Also worth considering: dealer financing often ties the loan to the purchase, so you’re locked into that dealer’s pricing and add-ons. A bank loan separates the car price from the financing, which can make negotiation easier. You can shop the car price down, then take that number to the bank. That separation is a big part of why the bank can be cheaper.

I’d be careful about assuming a lower rate always means a cheaper deal. The real comparison should be total cost over the loan term, including the purchase price and fees. If the dealer’s rate is subsidized, the bank can still win on total cost, especially if the dealer’s package includes extras that raise the amount financed.

So my take is that the headline dealer rate is a marketing number, not the full cost. The bank is cheaper when the total out-of-pocket over time is lower, even if its stated rate is higher. That’s the practical point: compare total cost, not just the percentage.

What strikes me most is how state law doesn't tell the whole story. Yes, a bunch of states have legalized medical marijuana, and some have legalized it recreationally too, but the federal government still treats it as a Schedule I drug. That gap is why a state can say "go ahead and smoke it" while the feds can technically call it illegal. I don't care as much about the philosophical "is it a drug?" debate. What matters is the inconsistency: you can buy it on a corner in a legalized state, yet the same plant can be a federal violation. It's like a legal tangle that keeps dragging.

Honestly, this question always makes me cringe because people imagine your heart is a tiny battery. It isn’t. What’s actually happening is ions moving through pores in cell membranes, and that movement creates tiny voltage differences. Sodium rushing in and potassium rushing out is the whole trick; it’s not a generator, it’s chemistry doing electrical work. I’d say the “exactly” part is simpler than people think: a nerve cell fires when the voltage flips for a split second, then it has to reset before it can fire again. No lightning, no magic, just membranes and ions doing their thing.

The short version is that sampling is about curation, not the clicking around. I've spent enough time in DAWs to know that the actual steps, pulling a file out of an old record, cleaning up the hiss, dropping a loop under a beat, are almost mechanical. The part that separates a track that works from one that feels like a collage of leftover scraps is the ear. You're not looking for the whole song; you're looking for the eight-second sliver of a 1972 soul record that, pitched down a few semitones and slowed to match your tempo, makes the whole thing breathe. That's where the craft lives, and honestly it's the part most people underestimate.

A typical workflow is pretty simple in outline: you get hold of the source, which might be a vinyl rip, a CD, or a digital file, load it into a sampler, chop out a loop, and layer it under new drums and bass. You'll usually clean the audio first, because old recordings carry hiss, crackle, and a bit of room noise, and you want the loop to sit clean in the mix. Then you adjust pitch and tempo so the sample fits your key and your beat instead of clashing with it. Often the best part isn't even in the main section of the song; you end up hunting through the B-side or the tail of the track for a drum fill or a spoken-word fragment nobody else has used. The trickier creative move is knowing when to leave it alone, because a sample that's been pitched and stretched too far sounds like it's fighting the track.

Where people get tripped up is the legal side, which I think is underplayed. You generally need to clear two rights: the publishing rights to the composition and the master recording rights to the actual performance. If you skip that, you're gambling on the original owner not coming for you. Some artists sample quietly and get away with it for years; others get a cease-and-desist or have to pay up and share royalties. My take is you should budget for clearing before you build a whole record around a snippet, not after.

So to answer your question directly: you sample by isolating a short loop, cleaning it, and re-pitching or re-temping it into a new arrangement. The technology is the easy part; the taste and the paperwork are where the real work is. I'd rather spend an afternoon hunting for the right four seconds than fiddle with the audio tools.

I get tension headaches more than I'd like. For years, I figured it was just my head being dramatic. But the honest answer, at least for me, is simpler and more physical than that. It's mostly muscles and nerves. When I'm stressed or staring at a screen too long, the muscles around my temples and neck tighten. That tightening puts pressure on the nerves that wrap around the skull. Add in a bit of vessel dilation, and suddenly those nerves start sending pain signals. The brain doesn't process pain exactly where the trigger is, which is why the pain can feel like it's spreading across the whole skull, not just where I'm clenching. I'm not a doctor, but that's the explanation that finally made sense to me. It's also why taking a break from the screen, drinking water, and relaxing my neck actually help most of the time.

I can’t even tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We got there at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, picked this place because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and thought it’d be easy. We put our names on their totally useless digital waitlist, and then we were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but then just stood around until 8:40 p.m. before someone casually said we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15. And this was for two people, with not a single solution offered. Honestly, if the wait’s going to stretch that far past payment, just tell people up front so the whole night isn’t wasted. It was a total disaster. If zero stars were an option, that’s what I’d give it.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly, there was no line at all. Two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than I expected to pay at one. Honestly, I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered; at that price I had assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but I feel like you can find those things at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us, so I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either; it reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any.

Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.

I'm giving it four stars, and keeping it. The spacebar has a rattle; hitting it with thumb edge makes it sound like a loose pen cap in a drawer. E key also repeats now and then, so “example” comes out as “eexample” and I have to backspace. That happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I’m typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it for the switches. I asked the seller what they were, and answer took a week. By then I had already pried off a keycap and checked myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don’t ache by the end anymore. That mattered to me more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I’d have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the spacebar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas basically my whole life. Well, the under-21 version of it, so no gambling. I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

The good part is the circular stage. It’s genuinely smart. You’re looking down into it, so from basically any seat you get a decent view, which is rare in Vegas. Some of the acts are impressive too, like the strength stuff, the aerialists, and the divers. Those people are real athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not exactly a rip-off, just that if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with a bit more clarity.

And clarity is the problem, to me. What’s the story? I still don’t know. A dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never really says what it’s trying to say. There’s also way too much happening at once, too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would have hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Quick ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal. $99 instead of the normal $125, which helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago I ordered two shirts for my dad from Rockmount Ranch Wear by phone. The shirts never showed up because the rep misread the address. Her handwritten 7 got read as a 1, so instead of going to 5407, they were sent to 5401. The 5401 residents took it to the local UPS store for return. Then it just vanished and we never heard anything more. It took us several weeks to figure out what happened. In the middle of that dispute, I placed a second order for two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the first two. The owner took the case then. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly to blame because we hadn't been friendly enough to the 5401 folks, only four doors away. Anyway, I disputed the original charge with my credit-card company, and eventually got the credit.
